concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the single requested research target.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpointing
concepts.reason: Automatic triggers, thresholds, and disabling conditions directly control checkpoint execution.

concepts.name: WAL commit-hook interaction
concepts.reason: Registering a commit callback can disable the configured automatic checkpoint mechanism.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE
concepts.reason: This mode defines checkpoint progress without waiting for readers or writers.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL
concepts.reason: This mode has distinct writer and reader conditions for checkpointing all frames.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART
concepts.reason: This mode adds a reader condition that enables the next writer to restart the WAL.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE
concepts.reason: This mode adds physical WAL truncation before a successful return.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP
concepts.reason: This mode exposes checkpoint status while checkpointing zero frames.

concepts.name: Reader boundaries and incremental checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader end marks constrain copying and explain why checkpoint work may require later invocations.

concepts.name: Checkpoint starvation
concepts.reason: Sustained reader overlap can prevent WAL reset and cause continuing WAL growth.

concepts.name: WAL reset and reuse
concepts.reason: Checkpoint completion, WAL reuse, and file truncation have different conditions.

concepts.name: Checkpoint synchronization and durability
concepts.reason: Synchronization ordering and synchronous settings determine checkpoint durability behavior.

concepts.name: Checkpoint scheduling and latency
concepts.reason: Executing a checkpoint in the committing thread can increase commit latency.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locking and busy handling
concepts.reason: Lock acquisition and busy-handler outcomes determine whether an attempted checkpoint can finish.

concepts.name: Checkpoint status counters
concepts.reason: Frame counters require distinct interpretations for successful calls, non-WAL databases, and multiple database targets.

concepts.name: Checkpoint database selection
concepts.reason: The checkpoint API selector determines which attached WAL databases an invocation targets.

concepts.name: SQLite write-ahead logging
concepts.reason: This is the parent mechanism, whose broader operation exceeds the requested checkpointing scope.

concepts.name: WAL reader snapshot selection
concepts.reason: Selecting page versions for reads is a sibling WAL operation, while its checkpoint constraints are covered under reader boundaries.

concepts.name: WAL write and commit processing
concepts.reason: Appending changes and commit records is a separate WAL operation outside the requested checkpoint mechanism.

concepts.name: Rollback journaling
concepts.reason: This alternative journaling approach is outside the checkpointing subtree.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers WAL content back into the original database file.
claims.quote: A checkpoint operation takes content from the WAL file and transfers it back into the original database file.

claims.text: Every new database connection enables automatic checkpointing with a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT value.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: For positive N, sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) automatically checkpoints a database on connection D after a commit leaves its WAL with at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: The wal_autocheckpoint pragma can be used to invoke this interface from SQL. Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE .

claims.text: By default, closing the last database connection on a database file triggers a checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for database readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits for no database writer and for all readers to use the most recent snapshot before checkpointing all log frames.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until all readers use only the database file so the next writer can restart the WAL from the beginning.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE extends SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART by truncating the WAL to zero bytes immediately before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP always checkpoints zero frames.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop before transferring a WAL page past the end mark of any current reader.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: A subsequent checkpoint invocation resumes WAL-to-database copying from progress recorded in the wal-index.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: If overlapping WAL-using read transactions keep at least one reader active, checkpoint starvation can allow unbounded WAL growth.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader-induced checkpoint starvation can be avoided by attempting checkpoints during gaps when no process is reading the database.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The writer rewinds the WAL when all WAL content has been transferred into the database and synced and no readers are using the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Checkpointing must sync the WAL to persistent storage before transferring its content into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: In WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync operation.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Under the default checkpoint policy, a COMMIT that triggers a checkpoint can be much slower because its thread also executes the checkpoint.
claims.quote: same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: If another process is checkpointing the same database, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() cannot obtain its exclusive checkpoint lock and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART, and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE also acquire an exclusive writer lock.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: For a successful call targeting one WAL database, a non-NULL pnLog receives the total number of frames in its log.
claims.quote: If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file

claims.text: For a successful call targeting one WAL database, a non-NULL pnCkpt receives the count of checkpointed frames in the log, including frames checkpointed before the call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: If zDb is NULL or an empty string, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() attempts the requested operation on all WAL databases attached to the connection.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by that interface.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Registering a sqlite3_wal_hook() callback disables automatic checkpointing previously configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: While SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL is pending, new database readers are allowed to proceed.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART does not impede readers while it is pending.
claims.quote: Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: A checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file, unless journal_size_limit is set.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set).

claims.text: In the WAL configuration described with PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, committed transactions can roll back after a power failure or hard reset.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

claims.text: If a concurrent checkpoint prevents obtaining the checkpoint lock, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() does not invoke the configured busy-handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: If the busy-handler returns 0 before acquiring the writer lock or while waiting for readers, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART, and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE fall back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: A checkpoint taking the documented busy-handler fallback to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: When zDb names an attached database outside WAL mode, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() returns SQLITE_OK with both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: When one sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() call targets all attached WAL databases, its pnLog and pnCkpt outputs are undefined.
claims.quote: then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

limitations: All supplied sources are primary SQLite documentation from one origin, so they cannot satisfy independent-origin source floors; S2 and S3 govern their specific C API semantics.
S1's three-mode summary is not exhaustive relative to S2's five documented modes; S1's isolated RESET label does not establish an additional mode.

S1 says RESTART/TRUNCATE ensure completion and may block readers, whereas S2 permits busy-handler fallback and SQLITE_BUSY and explicitly says RESTART does not impede readers; retained mode claims follow S2, and the packet supplies no historical reconciliation.
The packet does not establish checkpoint-mode introduction dates or compatibility with a particular deployed SQLite version.
Passes represent frozen-packet extraction and negation review, with new_information_rate defined as new_claims divided by cumulative total_claims; no retrieval rounds or saturation are claimed.
